options.text: An atom or group of atoms that carries an electric charge
options.explanation: Losing or gaining electrons leaves the particle charged; that charged particle is the ion.

options.text: An atom that has gained or lost protons
options.explanation: Protons stay fixed in the nucleus; ions differ only in their electrons.

options.text: An atom with extra neutrons
options.explanation: Neutron changes make isotopes, not ions - a different idea entirely.

options.text: Any atom with a full outer shell
options.explanation: Noble gases have full shells but no charge; charge, not fullness, makes the ion.

questions.stem: Why do atoms lose or gain electrons?

options.text: To reach a full outer shell of electrons
options.explanation: The full outer shell is the stable target; the charge is the side effect.

options.text: To turn into a noble gas element
options.explanation: The electronic structure matches a noble gas, but the particle stays the same element.

options.text: To balance the protons in the nucleus
options.explanation: The proton count never changes during ion forming.

options.text: To become electrically neutral
options.explanation: Neutral is the starting point; the whole point of the trade is ending up charged.

questions.stem: A sodium atom loses its single outer electron. Which noble gas does its electronic structure then match?

options.text: Neon
options.explanation: Sodium at 2,8,1 drops to 2,8 - neon's own arrangement.

options.text: Helium
options.explanation: Helium holds only 2 electrons; sodium's ion keeps two full shells beneath.

options.text: Argon
options.explanation: Argon sits at 2,8,8; sodium's ion has one shell fewer than that.

options.text: Krypton
options.explanation: Krypton is two shells larger still; nothing in sodium's loss reaches it.

questions.stem: Which statement covers every metal and every non-metal in ion forming?

options.text: All metals lose electrons; all non-metals gain them
options.explanation: The note states the rule without exceptions: metals lose, non-metals gain.

options.text: Metals gain and non-metals lose
options.explanation: Backwards - the losing side is always the metal.

options.text: Both lose electrons at the same time
options.explanation: If both lost, neither could accept; the exchange needs one giver and one taker.

options.text: Only some metals take part
options.explanation: The rule is all metals - there are no bystander metals here.

questions.stem: How does the charge of an ion relate to the electrons moved?

options.text: The charge equals the number of electrons gained or lost
options.explanation: Two electrons lost gives 2+, and 1 electron gained gives 1- - the count and the charge always match.

options.text: The charge equals the outer-shell total
options.explanation: The outer-shell total sets how many move, not the charge itself.

options.text: The charge is always 1, whatever moves
options.explanation: Charges of 2+ and 3- exist wherever two or three electrons move.

options.text: The charge equals the proton count
options.explanation: Protons fix the element, not the ion's charge; electrons decide the charge.

questions.stem: Name the three noble gases the note names for electronic structures.
State what every metal atom does in ion forming, and what every non-metal atom does.
questions.modelAnswer: Every metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positive ion; every non-metal gains electrons and becomes a negative ion.

questions.stem: Explain why an atom that gives up electrons ends up with a positive charge.
questions.modelAnswer: Because electrons are negative — losing them leaves more protons than electrons, so the particle's overall charge is positive.

questions.stem: An oxygen atom has 8 electrons (2,6) and gains 2 more. State the ion's charge and the noble-gas structure it now matches.
questions.modelAnswer: The ion carries a 2- charge and matches the 2,8 structure of neon.

options.text: A negative ion with more electrons than protons
options.explanation: Gaining electrons tips the balance negative; the extra electrons make the anion.

options.text: A positive ion with more protons than electrons
options.explanation: That describes a cation - the name swap catches learners who mix the two labels.

options.text: An atom that has gained protons
options.explanation: Protons never transfer between atoms; only electrons move when ions form.

options.text: A neutral atom with a full outer shell
options.explanation: A full outer shell often follows ion forming, but the particle is charged, not neutral.

questions.stem: What happens to metal atoms when they take part in ion forming?

options.text: They lose electrons and become positive ions
options.explanation: Every metal loses electrons; shedding them leaves more protons than electrons.

options.text: They gain electrons and become negative ions
options.explanation: That is the non-metal route; metals sit on the losing side.

options.text: They share electrons with non-metals
options.explanation: Sharing belongs to covalent bonding, a different subtopic.

options.text: They stay neutral because metals are stable
options.explanation: Metals do not keep their outer electrons; they hand them over and charge up.

questions.stem: A magnesium atom loses 2 electrons. What charge does the ion carry?

options.explanation: Each lost electron adds one positive unit: two electrons lost, so 2+.
The negative sign belongs to gains; losing electrons cannot leave a negative charge.
The count is two lost electrons, not one; the charge counts every electron moved.
Losing electrons always leaves a charge; neutrality belonged to the atom before the loss.

questions.stem: A bromine atom gains 1 electron. What charge does the ion carry?

options.explanation: One extra electron means one negative unit, so the ion is 1-.
Gains make negative ions; a positive sign would mean a loss.
Seven is the outer-shell count, not the charge; only gained electrons count.
The gained electron changes the balance; the ion cannot stay neutral.

questions.stem: In the note's chloride diagram, what does the chlorine atom do to reach a full outer shell?

options.text: It gains 1 electron and becomes Cl-
options.explanation: Non-metals gain; one electron in gives the chloride ion its 1- charge.

options.text: It loses 1 electron and becomes Cl+
options.explanation: Losing is the metal behaviour; chlorine takes the gaining route.
options.misconception: metal behaviour applied to a non-metal

options.text: It gains 7 electrons
options.explanation: Filling the shell needs one electron, not seven; the last shell is one short.

options.text: It loses its whole outer shell
options.explanation: Shells are not discarded; electrons are transferred one or two at a time.

questions.modelAnswer: A cation is a positive ion that forms when an atom loses electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.

questions.stem: State the charge on the magnesium ion and on the bromide ion from the lesson's examples.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium loses 2 electrons for a 2+ charge; bromine gains 1 electron for a 1- charge.

questions.stem: Explain why an anion carries a negative charge.
questions.modelAnswer: Because gaining electrons leaves more electrons than protons, so the overall charge is negative.

questions.stem: Aluminium (Group 3) reacts with sulfur (Group 6). State which element forms the cation, which forms the anion, and each ion's charge.
questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium is the cation at 3+ (a Group 3 metal donating its three outer electrons); sulfur is the anion at 2- (a Group 6 non-metal receiving two electrons).
